extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, federal courts, regulated utilities and their legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Legal comments arguing the limits of EPA authority under Clean Air Act Section 111(d), assessing statutory interpretation, Chevron deference, BSER scope, and predicate requirements under Section 111(b). Intended to show why the Proposed Rule is unlawful as applied to coal-fired EGUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Section 111(d) regulation of sources regulated under Section 112
rubrics_metrics.description: The unambiguous effect of reading the House and Senate amendments to Section 111(d) so as to give both amendments effect is to prohibit EPA from regulating, under Section 111(d), emissions of any air pollutant from sources in a category that is already regulated under Section 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving effect to both amendments renders the Proposed Rule invalid because it purports to regulate coal-fired EGUs (a source category already regulated under Section 112 by the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards). EPA's contrary reading creates a version of Section 111(d) 'substantially less restrictive' than either amendment and would rewrite clear statutory terms (citing Util. Air Regulatory Grp. v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference only when Congress intended to delegate
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts apply the Chevron framework: first ask whether Congress has spoken to the precise question; if Congress has, the agency must follow the statute; if not, courts ask whether Congress implicitly delegated interpretive authority to the agency — only then does Chevron step two deference apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron deference is appropriate only where there is evidence Congress meant for the ambiguity to be resolved by the agency. A drafting error cannot supply a basis for Chevron deference because a mistake conveys no congressional intent (citing Mead and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct conflict between statutory provisions is legislative choice, not ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct conflict between statutory provisions is not the sort of ambiguity that warrants Chevron deference; resolving such conflict is a legislative choice, not statutory construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have warned Chevron is not a license for an agency to 'repair a statute that does not make sense' (citing Scialabba (Roberts, C.J.) and Smiley/Citibank). Where provisions directly conflict, deference is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency interpretation must be reasonable and consistent with statutory purpose (Chevron step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chevron step two, courts will defer to an agency's interpretation only if it is reasonable and consistent with statutory purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's construction here contravenes congressional intent (to preclude duplicative/overlapping regulation of existing sources), is contrary to the statutory scheme avoiding double regulation, and would produce unfair economic results (stranded assets, undermining investments in pollution controls). Thus the interpretation is not reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 111(d) requires a valid Section 111(b) predicate rule for new sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d)(1)(A) directs that EPA require States to establish standards of performance for 'any existing source for any pollutant ... to which a standard of performance would apply if such source were a new source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may not issue regulations under Section 111(d) to regulate emissions from existing sources until it has adopted standards of performance under Section 111(b) for pollutants from new sources in the same source category. Proposed new-source rules that are invalid cannot serve as the predicate 111(b) rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of performance must reflect a BSER that is 'adequately demonstrated' (42 U.S.C. §7411(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'standard of performance' is 'a standard for emissions of air pollutants which reflects the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost ... and any non-air quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A system is 'adequately demonstrated' when it has been shown reasonably reliable, reasonably efficient, and reasonably expected to serve pollution control interests without becoming exorbitantly costly (Essex Chem.). An emissions standard based on technology not meeting that test (e.g., CCS as used in the Proposed New Source Rule) cannot be a valid 'standard of performance' and so cannot serve as an 111(b) predicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exclusivity of 'new source' and 'existing source' under Section 111
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 111(a), a source cannot be both a 'new source' and an 'existing source'; once an existing source is modified it becomes a 'new source' per Section 111(a)(2), and an 'existing source' is any stationary source other than a new source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's Proposed Modified and Reconstructed Source Rule improperly treats modified/reconstructed sources as both new and existing. EPA may not treat modified sources as 'new' for establishing a predicate rule yet 'existing' for subjecting them to continued regulation under an 111(d) standard; doing so is impermissible and creates perverse incentives to modify to avoid stricter standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER limited to technological and operational measures applicable to each affected facility (inside-the-fence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically and by text, 'system of emission reduction' is understood to mean technological and operational improvements that can be made at a specific unit (i.e., measures that reduce emissions during the operation of an affected facility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's Proposed Rule stretches BSER beyond these limits to include grid-wide measures (re-dispatch to other units, substitution with renewables/nuclear, demand reduction). Such outside-the-fence measures are not 'systems of emission reduction' applicable to individual facilities and therefore exceed Section 111(d) authority; only Building Block 1 (heat-rate improvements at units) attempts to meet the facility-level requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of performance must measure facility-level environmental performance, not aggregate category outcomes or demand-side shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance should logically be read to mean the amount of emissions attributable to a given generation output from a particular source; not the total emissions from a source category or reductions achieved by reducing demand or substituting other generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redefining 'performance' to allow shutting down or reducing use of particular units or forcing consumer behavior would permit EPA to regulate economic choices and infrastructure beyond its authority (illustrated by hyperbolic examples: banning gas lawnmowers, requiring paperless workplaces). Such redefinition is lawless and boundless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory definitions limit 'stationary source' to an individual building/structure/facility/installation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act and regulations define 'stationary source' as 'any building, structure, facility, or installation which emits or may emit any air pollutant' (40 C.F.R. § 60.2); Section 111(d) standards and implementing regulations apply to designated facilities/units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards and compliance procedures must apply to individual units (designated facilities), including testing, recordkeeping, and 'increments of progress' to be taken by owners/operators of a designated facility. EPA's 'portfolio approach' that treats many facilities and consumers as a single source or bases standards on changes across an industry contravenes these definitions and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using outside-the-fence and beyond-the-source-category measures (averaging, trading, re-dispatch, demand reductions) as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures that achieve reductions only through coordination among multiple facilities—emission averaging, allowance trading, demand-side reductions, re-dispatching generation from one facility to another—do not constitute a 'system of emission reduction' for an individual affected facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three of EPA's four proposed Building Blocks rely on such coordinated, industry-wide measures; relying on these to define BSER effectively defines the entire category and consumers as a single source, which is not permitted under Section 111(d) and implementing regulations.
